 ( Glenn James ) As 'Nellie Night' nears, we have memories galore about the great dog-whisperer
 Eddie Sefko November 17, 2026 2:00 PM CST To say Don Nelson was a dog person wouldn’t quite be accurate. 
 He was a rescue-dog person. In fact, he was a rescue-dog’s best friend. Nellie had a lot of them, many when he was coaching the Mavericks in the 1990s and 2000s.
 People who were with the organization then remember Lucky – the mixed-breed sidekick that Nellie brought along with him almost everywhere, including practices.
 One day, Lucky did what dogs sometimes have to do – right in the middle of the locker room. It was not a comment on the way the Mavericks were playing, just human nature (or canine nature). Although, Nellie would not have been afraid to use the analogy if it was appropriate.
 Sarah Melton was the Mavericks’ vice president of communications during most of Nelson’s time as coach and she became a close confidant and friend of the NBA’s second-winningest all-time coach. She was affectionately known as “Smiles” by Nelson, presumably from the immensely popular Hall & Oates song “Sara Smile.”
 Melton’s job required her to know all the habits and quirks that Nelson had. And there were many. She also had to befriend all his dogs.
 “He always had adopted dogs,” Melton said. “When I first started at the Mavs in 1999, one of my jobs was to write the game notes and one weekend I was in the office at Reunion Arena in the morning and nobody else was there.
 “All of the sudden, I smelled smoke. And I was wondering if the building was on fire. Then, a dog runs up to me at my desk. Nellie comes around the corner smoking a cigar, just roaming the hallways with his dog.”
 Nelson will be honored with “Nellie Night” at Wednesday’s Mavericks’ game against the Golden State Warriors. Those teams were two of his primary employers in a head coaching career that spanned 31 seasons and also included a lengthy stay in Milwaukee and a brief stop with the New York Knicks. He was with the Warriors for two coaching stints and was in Dallas from 1997 to 2005.
 Nelson had a way of making everybody’s job more fun. And he got away with a lot of things that others couldn’t. Or maybe they just weren’t bold enough to try.
 One day – actually several times – Nellie walked into practice at noon, wearing his golf gear – for a workout that was supposed to last until 1:30 p.m. He announced to the team:
 “OK, if somebody hits a half-court shot, practice is over.”
 Sure enough, five minutes later Nelson was out the door, heading to the golf course.
 But it was his love of dogs that made him seem more human than any of his coaching did. He had Lucky, Bella, Rosie, Girlie and some other dogs, one of whom had no apparent name because Nelson just called him “Mutt.”
 When the doctor told Nelson he had to lose some weight during the early 2000s, he started doing laps around the bowels of American Airlines Center. He would walk four times around the arena and that equaled one mile – all the while with Lucky at his side.
 When he was spending his offseason months in Hawaii, Nelson was at his most comfortable. And there were always dogs along for the ride, sometimes literally. The rotating poker nights, often at Willie Nelson’s Maui home, were legendary.
 One time, a visitor went with Nelson to the other Nelson’s house with a fresh $1,000 out of the local cash machine. When he got to the poker game, he realized Maui poker was a little different than the traditional games he’s taken part of in Las Vegas. After half of his bankroll was gone, he said "These games are crazy," and quickly tucked what was left of his money back in his wallet. Newcomers were treated like human ATMs at the Nelson & Nelson poker parties.
 I was that newcomer.
 “I love that he was a constant gambler,” Melton said. “If he was with a group out at lunch, you’d have to play credit-card roulette to see who would pay for lunch.”
 That’s part of the reason behind the promotion of giving the first 10,000 fans at Wednesday’s game a deck of commemorative Nellie playing cards.
 Melton retired from the Mavericks and now has her Texas real-estate license. That got her an invitation to stay at one of Nelson’s Maui properties. But Nellie had an ulterior motive, as was often the case. And the dogs played a big part in it.
 “Keith (her husband) and I were in the Bay Area for a wedding and we decided to extend the trip to Maui,” Melton said. “Nellie always offered one of his houses, but we had never been until then. He said the door would be unlocked. And it was.
 “He never locked up. There were poker guys, friends, dogs, all sorts of people coming in and out of that house. I had just gotten my real-estate license and he wanted me to look at a property he was thinking about buying.”
 This is where the story goes off the rails.
 “We go to this property – and it’s a golf course,” Melton said. “He thought since I’d passed six classes to get my license I could give him advice on what to offer for it. I mean, it’s a golf course. There were two courses, in fact. There was a private one, but next door was a public course he wanted to buy.
 “Nellie got us two golf carts – one for me and my husband and one for Nellie and Bella, his favorite dog at the time. Sometimes, she was on the cart, but mostly, she ran around the course, in the sand traps, into the water hazards, all over the greens. Only Nellie can get away with this kind of stuff.”
 The story wasn’t over. Nellie couldn’t take Bella through the clubhouse, so he told Sarah and her husband to go through the pro shop, buy something (and put it on Nellie’s tab) and meet him on the other side of the building.
 So Melton waited. And waited. And waited.
 “I’d forgotten my cell phone so I didn’t have his number,” she said. “We finally found somebody who knew Nellie and called him and he said: “Oh my gosh, senior moment.”
 Nellie had totally forgotten about Melton and her husband.
 “But he remembered Bella,” she said. “That’s how Nellie rolled.”
 Nelson was always finding ways to manipulate the system. If he was an accountant instead of a coach, you’d want him doing your taxes. He knew every loophole in the rules, which is why the NBA had to change the rulebook a time or two to adjust to Nelson’s strategies.
 Former San Antonio coach Gregg Popovich said at Nelson’s funeral service in August that when he got his first contract from the Spurs, it was Nellie who schooled Popovich on how to get an extra $50,000 per year out of the franchise. And the negotiating ploy worked. Over a five-year contract, that was an extra $250,000. “Enough to buy your house in San Antonio,” Popovich recalled Nellie saying.
 Personally, my favorite memories of Nelson came at a dimly lit hole-in-the-wall bar on Forest Lane in Dallas. I wish I had a dollar for every dollar I lost to Nellie on the shuffleboard table in the King’s X. He could shoot one mean game of shuffleboard, whether he was playing for a dollar or a hundred. It didn’t matter. He was as competitive as they come.
 And usually, one of his dogs was sleeping on the floor next to the table that held our beers and whatever money was at stake.
 Sometimes, you felt like Nellie had more tolerance for Lucky and his other rescue missions than he did for people. Maybe he did. Some of his players probably felt that way when they weren’t producing the way they were capable.
 But in almost every instance, they were almost always better for having been coached by Nellie. And that’s all he really wanted. I asked him once what he wanted on his tombstone and he simply said: “He was a pretty good coach.” And that he was. Just ask all the coaches who tried (and mostly failed) to outfox Nelson at the end of a close game.
